rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its root is the same shutting that gives close and cloister: claudere meant to shut a door, not merely to leave someone off a list. Exclusion is that same closing act, and a closed door makes a sound — which is why this house asks that the closing be stated, not left silent.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin excludere, ex- (out) plus claudere (to shut); the noun for the keeping-out.

rows.definition: Execute shortened to its shell name — the word for running a thing now.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The same following-through as execute, clipped down to fit a command line where every extra letter costs a keystroke. What exec asks for is not permission to run eventually, but the thing running now.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin exsequi, ex- plus sequi (to follow); exec is the modern clipping for carrying a thing out immediately.

rows.definition: To carry a thing out. Execution is where an instruction stops being words.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its root is a following, the same root behind sequence and consequence: to execute is to follow an instruction to its end, not to originate one. What executes answers to whatever it was given to carry out, step after step.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin exsequi, ex- (out) plus sequi (to follow).

rows.definition: The carrying out of what was planned. Execution is where a design meets what is actually there.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its root is a following all the way to the end, the same root as consequence: nothing is executed by will alone, only by tracking a plan through however reality answers back. Execution is where that following runs out of paper to walk on and has to cross real ground.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin exsequi, ex- (out) plus sequi (to follow); the noun for the carrying-out.

rows.definition: To be at all — the first fact about anything; in this house, already enough to be valued.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: To be at all. In this house, existing is already enough to be counted as worth valuing, before anything further is asked of it.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin existere/exsistere, ex- (out) plus sistere (to stand, to cause to stand), from stare (to stand).

rows.definition: Already there before this. Of what must be reckoned with rather than designed.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Already there before this moment arrived. What is existing must be reckoned with as it is, not simply designed around.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin existere/exsistere, ex- (out) plus sistere (to stand); the adjective for what is already standing.

rows.definition: Is, rather than is not. The assertion that a thing is there to be reckoned with.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its root is a standing-out, not a passive being: sistere meant to cause to stand, to plant something upright where it can be seen. What exists has, at root, been made to stand somewhere rather than merely happening to be.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin existere/exsistere, ex- (out) plus sistere (to stand); the third-person assertion of being.

rows.definition: To go out. An exit is what makes a place a room rather than a trap.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: In Latin the same word could also mean an outcome, even a death — the ending a path was always going to reach. An exit keeps only the gentler half of that old sense: not the end of everything, only the end of being inside.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin exitus, from exire (to go out), ex- plus ire (to go); the noun carried in Latin a further sense of an outcome or an ending, even a death, before English kept only the plainer sense of a way out.

rows.definition: Opened out to show what was folded away. The contents were always there; the state changed.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Opened out to show what had been folded away. Nothing new arrives when a thing expands; only the state of what was already there changes.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin expandere, ex- (out) plus pandere (to spread out); the verb moved from the literal spreading of a cloth or a wing to the general opening-out of anything that had been folded away, including a state waiting to be shown in full.

rows.definition: Growth outward into more room than before. Expansion adds reach and takes something to sustain.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its root also gives spawn, by way of Old French espandre: both words name a spreading-out from one point into many. Expansion is that same spread applied to room rather than to offspring, and it costs the same thing either way — more to sustain everywhere it now reaches.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin expandere, ex- (out) plus pandere (to spread out); the noun for the spreading-out.

rows.definition: What is anticipated in advance. Expectations shape what is noticed, which is why surprises are informative.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its root is a watching, not a guessing: exspectare named an active looking-out for something to arrive. An expectation is that same watch kept running in advance, and it is exactly what gets caught off guard when the watch turns out to be looking the wrong way.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin exspectare, ex- (out) plus spectare (to watch), from specere (to look).

rows.definition: Anticipated in advance. Expectation shapes what is noticed, which is why surprises are informative.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Anticipated in advance. What is expected quietly shapes what gets noticed, which is why the unexpected teaches more.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin exspectare, ex- (out) plus spectare (to watch), from specere (to look); the adjective for what was watched for in advance.

rows.definition: What it was like to undergo something. Experience is the one form of knowledge that cannot be transferred whole.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its root is a trial that risked something, not a fact observed safely from outside. What is known this way was earned by going through, which is exactly why no telling can hand the whole of it to someone who did not.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin experientia, from experiri (to try, to test), ex- plus a root related to peril and risk.

rows.definition: A deliberate trial arranged so its outcome will tell you something. An experiment must be able to disappoint you or it teaches nothing.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: It shares its whole root with experience: a trial that stakes something real on the outcome, not a safe rehearsal. An experiment that risks nothing is not really the same word wearing a lab coat.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin experientia, from experiri (to try, to test); a trial arranged to test what would otherwise stay unknown.

rows.definition: Deep capability in one domain, built by long practice. Expertise is knowing what matters here, which is why it does not transfer.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its root is the same trial that gives experience, worn down by repetition until it settles into something reliable: expertus names what has already been tested and found sound. What settles this way inside one domain is exactly what refuses to travel to another.
rows.historical_meaning: French expertise, from expert, from Latin expertus, the past participle of experiri (to try, to test).

rows.definition: Taking value from another without fair return or real consent. Exploitation is the thing this house's license names first and forbids outright.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A word that once named a plain accomplishment, an unfolding of work into result, before it hardened into the taking of value from another without fair return or real consent. This house's own license names that taking first among what it forbids outright.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French esploit (an accomplishment), from Latin explicitum, from explicare (to unfold), ex- plus plicare (to fold).

rows.definition: One who goes where they have not been in order to find out. An explorer accepts not knowing what they will meet.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The old grammarians read its second half as a cry, the shout a scout was said to raise on sighting what was sought, though that reading is tradition more than certainty. Even its own word is comfortable not knowing for sure, a fitting inheritance for one who goes looking without a guarantee of what they will meet.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin explorare (to search out, to scout); traditionally parsed as ex- plus plorare (to cry out), the cry a scout was said to raise on sighting what was sought, though that reading is the old grammarians' guess rather than a secured derivation.

rows.definition: To send a held thing out in a form others can use. Sovereignty over data begins with being able to export it.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its root is the same carrying that gives port and portable: to export is to make a held thing carriable again, fit to leave rather than sealed in a room. Sovereignty over data starts exactly there, at whether the carrying is allowed at all.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin exportare, ex- (out) plus portare (to carry).

rows.definition: Those that send held things outward in a usable form. Sovereignty over data begins with being able to export it.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Those parts of a system that carry held things outward in a usable form. What they guarantee is exactly the ability to leave with what was held.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin exportare, ex- (out) plus portare (to carry); the agent noun for what carries things outward.

rows.definition: To press what is inside into outward form — feeling or meaning given a body others can meet.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The pressing of what is inside into an outward form. Expression gives a feeling or a meaning a body that something else can meet.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin exprimere, ex- (out) plus premere (to press); to press what is inside outward into a form.

rows.definition: Puts outward what was inward. The word that reports an interior becoming shareable.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its root is a pressing under force, not a gentle offering: what expresses something has pushed hard enough for an inward thing to reach a surface. The verb reports the pressing in the act, not the shape it leaves behind.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin exprimere, ex- (out) plus premere (to press); the third-person form of pressing something outward.

rows.definition: The putting outward of what was inward. Expression is not decoration; it is how an interior becomes shareable.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The same pressing that leaves an impression or a print: exprimere names a squeezing-out under force, not a decorating-over. Expression is the mechanism by which what pressed for release actually reaches a surface another can read.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin exprimere, ex- (out) plus premere (to press); the noun for the putting-outward.

rows.definition: To reach further than before. Extension adds to what is there rather than replacing it.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its root is the same stretch that gives tendon and tension: a rope pulled longer without being cut. What extends reaches further along the line it already was, and stays whole the entire way.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin extendere, ex- (out) plus tendere (to stretch); the verb travelled from the literal stretching of a physical thing, a rope or a limb, to the more general reaching of anything, space, time, or a plan, beyond where it had stood before.

rows.definition: Something added that reaches further than the original. An extension belongs to what it extends.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its root is the same stretch that gives tension and tendon: an extension is a reaching pulled taut from something already whole, never a separate thing tied on. What is added this way answers to the tension of the thing it stretches from.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin extendere, ex- (out) plus tendere (to stretch); the noun for a stretching-further.

rows.definition: The outward faces of a thing, met before anything within. What the world sees without entering.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Grammatically its root is a comparative, not an absolute: exterior meant more-outward, one thing judged more outside than another rather than outside full stop. Exteriors are always outward relative to something they still belong to.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin exterior, the comparative of exter (outward), from ex (out of).

rows.definition: Belonging outside the bound. Of what is not ours to govern and must be reckoned with.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Belonging outside the bound of what is governed here. What is external must still be reckoned with, even though it answers to no rule of this house.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin externus, from exter (outward), from ex (out of).

rows.definition: To draw a part out of a whole. What is taken keeps its meaning; what it was taken from is left changed.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its root is the pull that once meant working a tooth or a splinter free: something held fast, loosened by force rather than handed over. What is extracted keeps the shape it had while it was still held, and the whole it came from keeps the gap.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin extrahere, ex- (out) plus trahere (to draw, to pull); the verb moved from the physical pulling of one thing free of another, a tooth or a splinter, to the more general drawing of any part out of any whole, including a fact out of a record.

rows.definition: The drawing of a part out of a whole. In this house the word carries a warning: extraction that takes without consent is what the license forbids.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The drawing of a part out of a whole. This house's own license carries a warning in the word: extraction that takes without consent is exactly what it forbids.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin extrahere, ex- (out) plus trahere (to draw, to pull); the noun for the drawing-out.
